prompt: A notebook model isn't automatically production-ready.
What gap does MLOps close?
explanation: A model that scores well in a Jupyter notebook can still fail once real traffic hits it, because production needs monitoring, versioning, and reliable pipelines the notebook never had.

prompt: A notebook model is automatically reliable in production.
explanation: Getting good numbers in a notebook says nothing about how the model behaves under real traffic, scale, or messy live data.

prompt: MLOps is mainly about closing the ___ gap.
Which is a real production concern MLOps addresses?
Which problems does MLOps help solve?
Working code alone guarantees production reliability.
explanation: Reliability also depends on monitoring, retraining, and handling live data that looks different from training data.

prompt: Why can a notebook model fail in production?
The ML lifecycle is a continuous ___.
Order the ML lifecycle loop steps.
explanation: For example, a fraud-detection model gets retrained every month as spending patterns shift — after retrain, the cycle starts back at train instead of ever finishing.

prompt: Monitoring happens only once, at the start.
What comes right after deploy in the loop?
After monitoring detects decay, teams often ___.
Which are stages in the ML lifecycle loop?
The ML lifecycle loop feeds back into itself.
Order these three loop stages.
Why is it called a 'loop' not a line?
Reproducing a result needs more than just code.
What must you fix to reproduce an ML result?
explanation: Re-running the same training script six months later with an updated library version can silently change the accuracy, even though the code itself never changed.

prompt: Code alone is enough to reproduce a result.
A different library ___ can change results silently.
Which factor also affects reproducibility?
Sort each item into its category.
options: Training data↔Must Fix|Library version↔Must Fix|Variable naming↔Doesn't Matter|Code comments↔Doesn't Matter

prompt: A fixed random seed helps reproduce results.
Which change could break reproducibility?
Why track environment versions?
explanation: When everyone trains with the exact same library versions, the same code produces the same result — that's what environment tracking buys you.

prompt: Data versioning tracks the exact ___ used for training.
What does data versioning let you retrieve later?
explanation: A tool like DVC snapshots a dataset the way git snapshots code, so you can check out the exact CSV a model was trained on six months ago.

prompt: Data versioning treats datasets like git treats code.
Why version training data?
Without data versioning, an old result may be ___.
An unversioned dataset can change without notice.
What does versioning data protect against?
What's a real tool for data versioning?
Match each tool to what it versions.
An experiment tracker logs runs automatically.
What does an experiment tracker log per run?
explanation: Instead of naming files 'model_v3_final_REALFINAL.pt' and hoping to remember the settings, a tracker automatically records the learning rate, batch size, and accuracy for every run.

prompt: Spreadsheets scale well for hundreds of experiments.
explanation: A spreadsheet gets unmanageable fast once you're comparing dozens of runs with many parameters each — that's exactly what a tracker automates.

prompt: An experiment tracker replaces manual ___ naming.
What problem does tracking solve?
What does a tracker typically record?
A run's parameters and results are stored together.
Sort each item by whether it's logged.
options: Learning rate↔Logged|Accuracy score↔Logged|Employee birthday↔Not Logged|Office location↔Not Logged

prompt: Why compare runs in a tracker?
MLflow Tracking is a real tracking tool.
What does MLflow Tracking record per run?
explanation: Calling mlflow.log_param('lr', 0.01) and mlflow.log_metric('accuracy', 0.93) inside a training script saves both to a run you can later browse in MLflow's web UI.

prompt: MLflow is open source.
How do you browse past MLflow runs?
In MLflow, log_metric() saves a run's ___.
MLflow runs cannot be compared to each other.
explanation: MLflow's UI is built specifically to let you compare runs side by side — that's a big part of the point.

prompt: What is an MLflow 'run'?
What can MLflow Tracking store per run?
Match each MLflow term to its meaning.
options: Param↔Input setting logged|Metric↔Result value logged|Artifact↔File output saved

prompt: W&B sweeps automate hyperparameter search.
What does a W&B sweep automate?
explanation: A sweep launches many training runs automatically — trying different learning rates or batch sizes — then W&B's dashboard shows which combination scored best.

prompt: A sweep tries many hyperparameter combos automatically.
A W&B ___ automates hyperparameter search.
What might a sweep search over?
Pick things a sweep can vary.
A sweep only ever runs training once.
explanation: A sweep's whole point is running many training attempts automatically, not just one.

prompt: What picks the best sweep result?
explanation: The sweep dashboard ranks runs by whichever metric you chose, like validation accuracy.

prompt: Staging and production are registry stages.
Pick model registry lifecycle stages.
explanation: A model moves from Staging (being tested) to Production (serving real traffic), then eventually Archived once a newer version replaces it.

prompt: Order registry stages, earliest first.
Match stage to what it means.
Archived means retired from serving.
A model in ___ serves real traffic.
Which stage comes right before Production?
Marketing is a registry lifecycle stage.
explanation: Marketing isn't a model lifecycle stage — the real ones are Staging, Production, and Archived.

prompt: Online feature stores serve real-time predictions.
What does an online feature store serve?
explanation: When a fraud model scores a transaction in milliseconds, it pulls features from the online store. The same features live in the offline store for training — keeping both in sync avoids training-serving skew, when training and live features quietly drift apart.

prompt: Offline stores serve model training.
The ___ store serves real-time predictions.
Which store is used at training time?
Match store type to its use.
Pick traits an online store needs.
Feature stores help prevent training-serving skew.
Sort each use into store type.
options: Model training↔Offline|Real-time scoring↔Online|Nightly batch job↔Offline|Fraud check API↔Online

prompt: A Feast FeatureView groups related features.
What does a Feast FeatureView group?
explanation: A 'driver_stats' FeatureView might group avg_rating and trips_today, since both come from the same underlying table — so Feast can serve them together as one unit.

prompt: A FeatureView bundles features from one source.
A Feast ___ groups related features.
Example grouped features in one FeatureView?
Pick things a FeatureView can group.
Grouping features avoids repeating ___.
A FeatureView can group unrelated secrets.
explanation: A FeatureView is meant to group related features from the same source, not random unrelated secrets.

prompt: A DAG has no cycles.
What must a DAG never contain?
explanation: A training pipeline DAG might run fetch-data, then validate, then train, then evaluate. Each step depends on the one before it, and nothing loops back — that's what makes it a DAG, a directed acyclic graph.

prompt: DAG stands for directed acyclic graph.
A DAG has no ___.
Order this pipeline, first step first.
Why avoid cycles in a pipeline?
A DAG step can depend on earlier steps.
Match pipeline step to its job.
options: Fetch data↔get raw data|Validate↔check data quality|Train↔fit the model|Evaluate↔score performance

prompt: Orchestration runs steps in the right ___.
Each Kubeflow Pipelines step runs in a container.
How does each Kubeflow pipeline step run?
explanation: A 'preprocess' component and a 'train' component each package their own code and dependencies into separate Docker containers, so they can run on different machines in the cluster without dependency conflicts.

prompt: Kubeflow components can run on different machines.
Each Kubeflow step runs in its own ___.
Why package steps as separate containers?
Pick benefits of containerized steps.
Kubeflow Pipelines runs on Kubernetes.
Kubeflow runs steps on a ___ cluster.
A DAG is a directed, ___ graph.
DAG stands for directed ___ graph.
explanation: Airflow pipelines are written as DAGs — tasks point to what runs after them, with no loops back.

prompt: A DAG can loop back to an earlier task.
explanation: That loop back is exactly what 'acyclic' rules out.

prompt: DAG tasks run in dependency ___.
Why must a DAG avoid cycles?
Airflow pipelines are written as DAGs.
Prefect pipelines feel more like plain Python.
What makes Prefect more Pythonic than Airflow?
explanation: Airflow traditionally needs DAGs defined upfront in a fixed shape; Prefect flows are regular Python functions that can branch at runtime.

prompt: Airflow DAGs are traditionally defined upfront.
Prefect flows are just regular ___ functions.
Which is more rigid about pipeline shape?
What do Airflow and Prefect share?
explanation: Unlike Kubeflow Pipelines, which runs natively on Kubernetes, Airflow and Prefect are general-purpose orchestrators applied to ML work.

prompt: Orchestrators can auto-retry a failed task.
What happens when a task fails?
explanation: You set a retry count and delay, and the orchestrator reruns just that failed task instead of the whole pipeline.

prompt: A failed task always restarts the entire pipeline.
explanation: Only that one task retries, not the whole DAG.

prompt: You configure a retry ___ before giving up.
What retries after a task fails?
Retry delay is configurable.
A data check can block a bad merge.
What can a data quality gate block?
explanation: Beyond normal code tests, ML CI adds checks like schema validation or missing-value limits, failing the build if data looks wrong.

prompt: Data quality gates check things a normal test suite wouldn't.
A schema check catches unexpected column ___.
Pick genuine data quality checks.
Data quality gates run only after deployment.
explanation: They run in CI, before a merge or promotion, not after deployment.

prompt: A model gate can reject a worse model.
What does a model quality gate compare?
explanation: If the new model's accuracy (or another metric) falls below a set threshold, CI fails the build instead of promoting it.

prompt: A model gate compares against a set ___.
What happens if accuracy drops below threshold?
Model gates only check code style.
explanation: They check model performance metrics, not code style — that's what normal linting already covers.

prompt: Why compare against a baseline model?
ML CI adds steps beyond a normal test suite.
Complete: fail the build on low accuracy.
explanation: A quality gate is just an extra check step bolted onto a normal CI pipeline — same mechanics as any other pipeline step, just a new condition.

prompt: ML CI reuses the same pipeline mechanics as normal CI.
ML CI adds ___ on top of normal tests.
What triggers an ML quality gate check?
A quality gate step can stop a pipeline early.
A retraining job can run on a fixed schedule.
Complete: cron for every Sunday midnight.
explanation: This cron trigger fires the retraining pipeline once a week — the same schedule syntax used for cron jobs anywhere, not something ML-specific.

prompt: Scheduled retraining runs regardless of recent data changes.
explanation: It just fires on a timer — whether retraining was actually needed is a separate question.

prompt: A scheduled trigger fires on a fixed ___.
What kind of trigger is 'every Sunday'?
Cron syntax was invented specifically for ML.
explanation: It's the same general-purpose scheduling syntax used across all kinds of automation.

prompt: Detected drift can trigger retraining.
What can trigger retraining besides a schedule?
explanation: Instead of waiting for the next scheduled run, a drift alert can kick off retraining immediately.

prompt: Drift-triggered retraining reacts to a clock.
explanation: It reacts to a detected drift signal, not a clock — that's the scheduled kind.

prompt: Drift-triggered retraining reacts to detected ___.
Why retrain on drift instead of waiting?
A pipeline can have more than one trigger type.
A challenger model must beat the champion to win.
What is a 'champion' model?
explanation: The newly retrained model is the 'challenger' — it only replaces the champion if it performs better on held-out data.

prompt: A challenger automatically replaces the champion.
explanation: It only replaces the champion if it wins the comparison — otherwise the champion stays live.

prompt: The newly retrained model is the ___.
When does a challenger get promoted?
Pick roles in a champion/challenger setup.
A model artifact includes the trained weights.
What is a model artifact?
explanation: Like a Docker image, but the payload is trained weights and metadata (like framework version) instead of app code.

prompt: A model artifact is just the training script.
explanation: The training script produces the artifact — the artifact itself is the trained weights and metadata.

prompt: A model artifact stores trained ___.
What metadata might an artifact include?
A model artifact can be versioned like code.
Inference code loads the model and predicts.
What does inference code do?
explanation: Packaging bundles the weights with the small amount of code that loads them and runs a prediction — without it, the weights alone are unusable.

prompt: Weights alone are unusable without inference code.
Inference code ___ predictions from input.
What gets bundled with model weights?
Inference code retrains the model each run.
explanation: Inference code only runs predictions — retraining is a separate process.

prompt: Pinning library versions avoids a training/serving mismatch.
Why pin exact library versions?
explanation: If serving uses a different library version than training, the same weights can produce different results — pinning keeps behavior consistent, the same idea Docker images use for OS packages.

prompt: An unpinned library version can change model output.
Pinning versions keeps training and serving ___.
What happens without pinned versions?
Version pinning is unique to machine learning.
explanation: It's a general packaging practice — ML just depends on it more, since even a small library version bump can shift predictions.

prompt: ONNX lets a model run across different frameworks.
What problem does a format like ONNX solve?
explanation: ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange) is a shared file format, so a model trained in one framework, like PyTorch, can be served by tools built for another.

prompt: Every framework requires its own unique file format.
explanation: A shared format like ONNX avoids that — one exported file can run in multiple serving tools.

prompt: ONNX is a shared model file ___.
Which is a cross-framework model format?
Exporting to ONNX can remove framework lock-in.
Batch inference scores data with no live request.
What is batch inference?
explanation: Batch inference runs on a pile of data all at once, like scoring last night's orders every morning — no user is waiting on a live response.

prompt: Batch inference responds instantly to one request.
explanation: That's online inference — batch runs on a schedule instead.

prompt: Batch inference processes data in ___.
Give an example use for batch inference.
Batch inference suits cases where latency doesn't matter.
Online inference answers one request at a time.
What defines online inference?
explanation: A live API call comes in, the model predicts, and a response goes back within milliseconds — like a fraud check during checkout.

prompt: Online inference is synchronous, request by request.
Online inference must respond with low ___.
Give an example of online inference.
Online inference tolerates multi-hour delays.
explanation: It needs to answer within a short window, often milliseconds — that's the whole point of 'online.'

prompt: Streaming inference reacts to a continuous event flow.
What does streaming inference process?
explanation: Predictions run continuously as new events arrive, like scoring transactions off a live event queue — a middle ground between batch's schedule and online's single request.

prompt: Streaming inference waits for a nightly schedule.
explanation: It reacts continuously as events arrive, not on a fixed nightly schedule — that's batch.

prompt: Streaming inference reacts to a live event ___.
Which pattern fits a live transaction feed?
Sort each workload by serving pattern.
options: Nightly report↔Batch|Fraud check API↔Online|Live transaction feed↔Streaming

prompt: TensorFlow Serving is built to serve TF models.
What is TensorFlow Serving for?
explanation: It exposes a trained TensorFlow model over gRPC or REST, handling versioning and swaps without you writing a server from scratch.

prompt: TensorFlow Serving trains new models.
explanation: It only serves already-trained models — training happens separately.

prompt: TensorFlow Serving exposes a model over gRPC or ___.
What does a model server save you from writing?
Predict the output: check model status.
explanation: Hitting a TF Serving REST endpoint reports whether the model version is loaded and ready, here AVAILABLE.

prompt: TorchServe is PyTorch's equivalent of TensorFlow Serving.
What is TorchServe built for?
explanation: Same idea as TensorFlow Serving, but for models trained in PyTorch.

prompt: TorchServe serves models trained in PyTorch.
TorchServe is TensorFlow Serving's PyTorch ___.
Which tool is TensorFlow's equivalent?
TorchServe and TensorFlow Serving solve the same problem.
Triton can serve models from multiple frameworks.
What makes Triton different from TorchServe?
explanation: NVIDIA Triton Inference Server can host TensorFlow, PyTorch, and ONNX models side by side on the same GPU-optimized server, instead of locking you into one framework.

prompt: Triton locks you into a single framework.
explanation: That's the opposite of its point — it serves multiple frameworks side by side.

prompt: Triton is optimized for ___ hardware.
Pick a genuine multi-framework server.
Pick real model serving tools.
A canary deployment starts with a small traffic slice.
What is a canary deployment?
explanation: Like a real canary release: maybe 5% of users get the new model version while 95% stay on the old one, so a bad version only affects a few people before you notice.

prompt: Canary deployments start with most traffic on new version.
explanation: A canary starts small — often just 1-5% — precisely so a bad version only hurts a few users.

prompt: A canary deployment sends a ___ of traffic first.
Why start a canary at low traffic?
Which metrics does a canary watch?
Complete: give the new version 5% of traffic.
explanation: A weight of 5 means 5% of live traffic goes to the canary version while the rest stays on the stable one.

prompt: Order the canary rollout steps.
explanation: If metrics look bad partway through, the rollout can also reverse — a rollback that sends all traffic back to the old version instead of continuing to ramp up.

prompt: Shadow deployment sends live traffic but ignores its output.
What happens to a shadow model's output?
explanation: The new model runs on real, live requests in parallel with production, but its predictions are only logged for comparison — real users never see them, so there's zero user-facing risk.

prompt: Shadow deployment carries zero user-facing risk.
explanation: Because its predictions never reach a real user, a shadow model can be badly broken without anyone but you noticing.

prompt: Shadow traffic is ___ real user traffic.
How is shadow different from canary?
What can shadow deployment help check?
A shadow model's output can reach a real user.
explanation: Its output is only ever logged for comparison, never returned to a real request.

prompt: Watching a model's output distribution can reveal problems.
What does output monitoring track?
explanation: Beyond the logs, metrics, and traces you'd track for any service, ML systems also need to watch the shape of what the model predicts — if a spam filter suddenly flags 90% of email as spam, that's a red flag even with normal latency and error rates.

prompt: Normal latency metrics catch every ML problem.
explanation: A model can be fast and error-free while still quietly predicting garbage — that's why output distribution needs its own watch.

prompt: ML monitoring watches prediction ___ over time.
A sudden shift in predicted classes signals?
Which of these is specifically ML monitoring?
explanation: Latency and disk space apply to any service — watching what a model actually predicts is the ML-specific layer on top.

prompt: Output distribution monitoring is unique to ML systems.
A model's confidence scores can be monitored too.
What is a confidence score?
explanation: It's the probability a model attaches to its own prediction — a spike in low-confidence predictions often shows up before accuracy even drops, since confidence shifts the moment inputs start looking unfamiliar.

prompt: Rising low-confidence predictions can warn of trouble early.
Confidence monitoring flags ___ predictions.
Why watch confidence instead of just accuracy?
explanation: Real accuracy needs the true outcome, which often arrives later — confidence is available the instant a prediction is made.

prompt: A confidence score near 50/50 means?
Confidence scores replace the need for ground truth.
explanation: They're an early warning signal, not a replacement — you still need real outcomes, the ground truth, to know if predictions were actually correct.

prompt: Data drift means input data has changed shape.
What is data drift?
explanation: Say a loan model was trained on applicants averaging age 35 — if most applicants are now 22, the input distribution has shifted even though the model itself never changed.

prompt: Data drift can happen without any code change.
Data drift is a shift in ___ data.
Data drift affects which side of a model?
Data drift alone always breaks predictions.
explanation: Feature values can shift while the model still handles them fine — drift is a warning sign to watch, not proof predictions broke.

prompt: A classic data drift example is?
Concept drift means the input-output link changes.
What is concept drift?
explanation: During a sudden shift like a pandemic, past purchase patterns stopped predicting future buying behavior — inputs looked similar, but what they meant for the correct output had genuinely changed.

prompt: Concept drift can happen with unchanged input data.
explanation: The features can look statistically identical while the correct answer for those same features quietly changes.

prompt: Concept drift changes what output ___ correct.
Concept drift differs from data drift how?
Concept drift is always easy to spot fast.
explanation: It often only shows up once real outcomes arrive

prompt: Concept drift means the same input now?
A drift score above a threshold flags an alert.
How is drift usually detected?
explanation: A common tool is PSI, the Population Stability Index — a single number comparing today's feature distribution to the training distribution; the bigger the number, the more the data has shifted.

prompt: A higher PSI score means less drift.
explanation: PSI grows as distributions diverge — a small PSI looks like training data, a large one means they've moved apart.

prompt: PSI compares today's data to the ___ data.
What does this drift check print?
options:
psi_score = compute_psi(train_dist, live_dist)
print('ALERT' if psi_score > 0.2 else 'OK')
# psi_score = 0.35|ALERT

prompt: A drift score is compared against a?
PSI needs the original training distribution to work.
Detected drift can trigger a retraining pipeline.
What often happens after drift is confirmed?
explanation: This is the same retraining-trigger idea from continuous training — instead of waiting on a fixed schedule, a confirmed drift alert can kick off training on fresh data right away.

prompt: Drift response always means discarding the model.
explanation: Often it just means retraining the same architecture on newer data — no need to throw anything away.

prompt: Drift can trigger a fresh ___ run.
Besides retraining, a drift alert can prompt?
Ignoring persistent drift usually improves accuracy.
explanation: Left unaddressed, drift tends to make predictions steadily less reliable as live data drifts further from training data.

prompt: A drift-triggered retrain uses which data?
Data validation tests check incoming data quality.
What do data validation tests check?
explanation: Beyond a normal unit test that checks your code's logic, a data validation test checks the data itself — like making sure an 'age' column never holds a negative number before it reaches the model.

prompt: Data validation tests run before training or inference.
Data validation catches bad data before the ___.
A data validation test might catch?
Data validation differs from a unit test by checking?
Schema checks are a form of data validation.
explanation: A schema check confirms columns have the right names, types, and shape — one of the most common data validation tests.

prompt: An invariance test expects output to stay the same.
What does an invariance test check?
explanation: Change something the model shouldn't care about — like swapping a loan applicant's name from 'John' to 'Maria' — and a fair model's approval decision should stay exactly the same.

prompt: An irrelevant edit changing output is a bug.
explanation: If flipping an unrelated detail flips the decision, that's exactly the kind of hidden bias a behavioral test is meant to catch.

prompt: Invariance tests change ___ inputs, expect the same result.
Behavioral tests mainly focus on a model's?
A directional test expects output to move?
explanation: Raising a house's square footage in a price model should predictably push the predicted price up, not down.

prompt: Invariance and directional tests are both behavioral tests.
A model card documents a model before it ships.
What is a model card?
explanation: It's a short standardized document covering a model's intended use, its training data, known limitations, and its measured performance — similar in spirit to a nutrition label, but for a model.

prompt: A model card lists a model's intended use.
A model card records known ___.
A model card is most like a?
What belongs on a model card?
Model cards are written after a model already failed.
explanation: They're meant to exist before a model ships, so anyone using it already knows its limits.

prompt: Some models need human sign-off before going live.
What is an approval workflow for?
explanation: A high-stakes model, like one deciding loan approvals, often needs a designated reviewer to sign off before it's promoted to production — the same instinct as a code review, applied to a model release.

prompt: Approval workflows apply mostly to high-stakes models.
Approval gates require a human ___.
An approval workflow is closest to a?
Skipping approval on a risky model risks?
Every internal experiment needs full approval sign-off.
explanation: Approval gates matter most for models that reach production and affect real people — not every early experiment needs the same ceremony.

prompt: A fairness check compares performance across groups.
What does a fairness check compare?
explanation: For example, checking whether a hiring model approves resumes at similar rates across genders — a model can look accurate overall while quietly performing worse for one subgroup.

prompt: A model can look accurate but still unfair.
Fairness checks compare results across ___.
A fairness check might reveal?
Fairness checks should mainly happen?
explanation: Ideally it's caught before shipping — governance is about catching gaps early, not reacting after harm is already done.

prompt: Fairness checks are unrelated to model governance.
explanation: They're actually a core part of governance — fairness is one of the things a responsible approval process checks for.

prompt: LLM apps need to version prompts like code.
What is prompt versioning?
explanation: The same instinct behind a model registry tracking which trained weights are live now applies to prompts too — an LLM app needs to know exactly which prompt text produced which behavior, and roll back a bad edit just as easily.

prompt: A prompt change can break app behavior.
Prompt versioning tracks changes over ___.
Prompt versioning borrows its idea from?
Without prompt versioning, a bad edit is hard to?
Prompts are stable enough to never need tracking.
explanation: A small wording tweak can noticeably change an LLM's answers, so prompts need the same careful tracking as model weights.

prompt: RAG answers are graded on real grounding.
What does RAG evaluation check?
explanation: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation — the model looks up real documents before answering. Evaluation checks whether the final answer is actually grounded in those documents, not just fluent-sounding text the model invented.

prompt: A fluent RAG answer can still be ungrounded.
explanation: An answer can read perfectly well while citing facts the retrieved documents never actually said — that's exactly what grounding checks catch.

prompt: RAG evaluation checks answers against retrieved ___.
RAG stands for retrieval-augmented?
Why can't tests assert one exact LLM answer?
explanation: The same prompt can produce differently-worded answers each run, which is why many teams grade LLM output with another model acting as a judge, instead of one fixed expected string.

prompt: An LLM-as-judge approach can score answer quality.
Token usage adds a new cost dimension to watch.
What is token cost monitoring?
explanation: Every LLM call is billed by tokens in and out, so on top of the prediction-distribution and confidence monitoring from earlier, LLM systems also need to watch cost per request — a subtle prompt change can quietly multiply your bill.

prompt: A longer prompt can directly raise token cost.
LLM calls are billed by ___ used.
Token cost monitoring is mostly unique to?
A cost spike might come from?
Token cost is irrelevant once accuracy looks fine.
explanation: A model can be accurate and still quietly burn far more budget than expected — cost is its own thing to watch, separate from correctness.

options: Canary↔Small traffic slice|Rollback↔Revert on bad metrics|Ramp-up↔Increase traffic gradually

options: Applicant ages shift↔Data drift|Same inputs, new correct label↔Concept drift|Buying habits change meaning↔Concept drift|Fewer young applicants apply↔Data drift

prompt: Match each ML test to what it checks.
options: Data validation↔Incoming data quality|Invariance test↔Output stays stable|Directional test↔Output moves predictably
